---
title: "Collection and testing"
order: 2
---

## The ticket

A whole blood unit is drawn from a donor at a Lakeshore Blood Center mobile site Tuesday
morning. The phlebotomist ties the donor, the collection bag, and a set of small sample tubes
together under one number before the needle ever goes in — the same number will follow this
donation through every record it generates from here forward. By Tuesday afternoon, the unit
has already moved to Lakeshore's processing lab and been spun down and split into three separate
products: red cells into a refrigerator, plasma into a freezer, platelets into a room-temperature
agitator in a different part of the building. Meanwhile, the sample tubes drawn alongside the
unit are in the testing lab, running through the infectious-disease and blood-typing panel that
has to clear before any of this becomes something a hospital can use.

Wednesday morning, one of those tests comes back reactive.

Now Lakeshore doesn't have one product to deal with. It has three — a bag of red cells, a bag of
plasma, and a bag of platelets, sitting in three different pieces of equipment, each one
traceable only by that same number assigned Tuesday morning. All three have to be found and
placed on hold before anyone downstream touches them, and the clock on that started the moment
the result posted, not whenever someone happens to notice. Understanding how Lakeshore finds all
three, and what stops any one of them from moving in the meantime, is what this module is about.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

The failure mode here is direct: a unit that carries a transfusion-transmitted infection, or the
wrong blood type, has to be stopped before it reaches a patient — and by the time a test result
comes back, the physical product it applies to may already be sitting in three different
locations, not one. If Lakeshore's control against that risk depended on *finishing testing
before doing anything else with the unit*, this scenario would be a crisis: real blood centers
don't work that way, because component shelf life is short and processing has to start fast to
get any usable product out of the collection at all. The actual control has to work regardless of
where the physical product is or how many pieces it's been split into.

You already know this shape of problem, just under a different name: **quarantine is a change
freeze, or a release gate, not a sequencing rule.** In change management, you don't necessarily
block every build or deployment activity until every check has run — you build, you test, you
stage, often in parallel — but you have one authoritative gate that nothing crosses into
production until every required check has passed and that pass/fail is recorded. The freeze isn't
about *when* work happens; it's about what's allowed to move forward before the gate opens. A
reactive infectious-disease result is a failed gate, and — this is the part that's easy to
underweight if you're thinking of it as just a red status flag — a failed gate here carries
downstream obligations a failed build never does: the donor has to be deferred and told why, and
in some cases, *every prior donation from that donor has to be traced and reviewed*, which is a
lookback investigation, not just a rejected release.

The mechanism that makes this work, operationally, is a status field — "quarantine status" —
attached to every product derived from a donation inside Lakeshore's Blood Establishment
Computer Software (BECS, the system of record you saw named in module 1 for donor eligibility;
here it's doing the equivalent job for product release), checked automatically before that
product can be released, shipped, or used, no matter where it physically sits. That's the part
worth sitting with: the control isn't "don't touch the unit until testing finishes." It's "no
product carrying this donation's identifier moves past release, regardless of what's already
happened to it physically, until BECS says the gate has opened."

## The rule, in plain English

Four things are true about every donation Lakeshore collects, and they run in parallel with each
other, not in sequence:

1. **The donation gets one identifying number that ties everything to it.** The donor, the
   collection bag, and every sample tube drawn alongside it are linked under a single number at
   the moment of collection — the record that lets Lakeshore later ask "which products came from
   this donation" and get a complete answer, even after the bag has been split into several
   physical products. (This number is the seed of something you'll get the full picture of in
   module 3: the Donation Identification Number, or DIN — a globally standardized identifier under
   a labeling system called ISBT 128. One sentence is all this module needs; the rest is module
   3's job.)
2. **Component separation can start almost immediately.** Whole blood collected Tuesday morning
   can be spun, separated, and moved into its component-specific storage the same afternoon — this
   is routine, not a shortcut, because red cells, plasma, and platelets each have very different
   shelf lives and processing windows that don't wait on a lab result. (Apheresis donation — where
   a machine draws blood, separates out only the component being collected, such as platelets, and
   returns the rest to the donor during the same visit — produces a more targeted product faster,
   but the identity and testing rules that follow are the same either way; this module doesn't go
   deeper into the apheresis-versus-whole-blood mechanics than that.)
3. **The sample tubes run through the required testing panel on their own timeline**, in the
   testing lab, independent of wherever the physical components have already gone. This includes
   the infectious-disease screening panel (tests for evidence of HIV, hepatitis B and C, and
   several other transfusion-transmitted infections) and the blood-typing work (ABO group, Rh
   factor, and a screen for unexpected antibodies).
4. **Nothing tagged with that donation's number is released, shipped, or used until every required
   result is in and passes.** That's the gate. It doesn't matter that the platelets have been
   sitting ready since Tuesday afternoon — if Wednesday's result is still pending, or comes back
   reactive, the platelets, the plasma, and the red cells are all still subject to the same hold,
   because they all still carry the same donation identifier.

If a result comes back reactive, three things happen, not one: every product from that donation
gets pulled from wherever it's sitting and quarantined or destroyed; the donor is deferred, and
depending on which test was reactive, further supplemental testing and a possible lookback into
that donor's prior donations may be triggered; and the donor is notified, the same obligation
module 1 covered for eligibility deferrals, now running on a reactive-test trigger instead.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.160(c) | "Six-oh-six point one-six-oh, paragraph c" | A donor number must be assigned to each accepted donor that relates the collected unit, the donor's medical record, and any component or product made from that unit, together. | The number assigned Tuesday morning that lets Lakeshore find the platelets, plasma, and red cells all from the same reactive donation, even after they've been split into three physical locations. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(1)(iii) | "Six-oh-six point one-six-oh, paragraph b, sub-one, clause iii" | Records must capture donor adverse reaction complaints and reports, including the results of investigation and followup. | If Tuesday's donor had a reaction during the draw — lightheadedness, a hematoma — that has its own record requirement, independent of whatever the sample tubes turn up later. |
| 21 CFR 610.40(a)(1)–(2) | "Six-ten point four-oh, paragraph a, sub-one and sub-two" | Each donation must be tested for evidence of infection due to a defined list of relevant transfusion-transmitted infections. | The panel running on Tuesday's sample tubes all day Tuesday and Wednesday morning — the work that produces the reactive result. |
| 21 CFR 606.40(a)(3), (4), (6) | "Six-oh-six point four-oh, paragraph a, sub-three, sub-four, sub-six" | A blood establishment's facilities must provide adequate space for storage of blood and components pending completion of testing, quarantine storage pending repeat testing of questionable results, and quarantine storage/handling/disposition of unsuitable products. | The physical and procedural reason "quarantine" is a real, defined status at Lakeshore, not an informal label — it's a facility requirement, not just a BECS field. |
| 21 CFR 610.40(g) | "Six-ten point four-oh, paragraph g" | Blood and blood components may be released or shipped prior to completion of infectious-disease testing only in documented medical emergencies or FDA-approved further-manufacturing cases — otherwise, testing has to be complete first. | The rule that keeps Tuesday afternoon's separated platelets sitting in quarantine rather than shipping, even though they're physically ready, because this isn't one of the narrow exceptions. |
| 21 CFR 610.40(h)(1) | "Six-ten point four-oh, paragraph h, sub-one" | Blood or blood components with a reactive screening test, or collected from a donor with a prior reactive result, must not be shipped or used, with narrow exceptions. | Wednesday's result — the specific rule that puts all three of Tuesday's products on hold at once, wherever they are. |

## The actual text

Start with the number that ties everything together — the one assigned before the needle goes
in — quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`:

> (c) A donor number shall be assigned to each accepted donor, which relates the unit of blood
> collected to that donor, to his medical record, to any component or blood product from that
> donor's unit of blood, and to all records describing the history and ultimate disposition of
> these products.

Read that plainly: one number, and everything derived from that donation — the medical record,
every component, every disposition record — has to trace back to it. That's the identity link
that lets Lakeshore's system find the plasma and the red cells the moment the platelets show up as
linked to a reactive donation, without anyone having to remember or manually search where each
product physically went.

The adverse-reaction record requirement, for the donor side of Tuesday's draw, from the same
source:

> (iii) Donor adverse reaction complaints and reports, including results of all investigations
> and followup.

Now the testing requirement itself, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/610.40.md`:

> (a) *Human blood and blood components.* Except as specified in paragraphs (c) and (d) of this
> section, you, an establishment that collects blood and blood components for transfusion or for
> use in manufacturing a product... must comply with the following requirements:
>
> (1) Test each donation for evidence of infection due to the relevant transfusion-transmitted
> infections described in § 630.3(h)(1)(i) through (iii) of this chapter (HIV, HBV, and HCV).
>
> (2) Test each donation for evidence of infection due to the relevant transfusion-transmitted
> infections described in § 630.3(h)(1)(iv) through (vii) of this chapter (HTLV, syphilis, West
> Nile virus, and Chagas disease)...

Notice the phrase "each donation" — not "each product." One donation, tested once at the sample
level, and the result has to govern every product that donation produced, however many pieces it
was split into by the time the result comes back.

The facilities requirement that makes "quarantine" a defined physical and procedural reality, not
an informal hold, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.40.md`:

> (3) The storage of blood or blood components pending completion of tests.
>
> (4) The quarantine storage of blood or blood components in a designated location pending
> repetition of those tests that initially gave questionable serological results.
>
> (6) The quarantine storage, handling and disposition of products and reagents not suitable for
> use.

Lakeshore's building itself, under this requirement, has to have somewhere specific for
Tuesday's platelets to sit while they're pending testing — and somewhere specific for them to sit
if Wednesday's result comes back questionable. This is why "quarantine" at a real blood center
means a designated location and a documented status, not just "someone remembered not to ship it."

The rule that keeps everything on hold by default, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/610.40.md`:

> (g) *Release or shipment prior to testing.* Human blood or blood components that are required
> to be tested for evidence of infection due to relevant transfusion-transmitted infections
> designated in paragraph (a) of this section may be released or shipped prior to completion of
> testing in the following circumstances provided that you label the blood or blood components
> under § 606.121(h) of this chapter, you complete the tests... as soon as possible after release
> or shipment, and that you provide the results promptly to the consignee:
>
> (1) Only in appropriately documented medical emergency situations; or
>
> (2) For further manufacturing use as approved in writing by FDA.

Read the structure of that paragraph carefully: it's written as an exception, which means the
default it's carving an exception *from* is "you don't release or ship until testing is
complete." Lakeshore's platelets sitting quarantined Wednesday morning aren't waiting because of
some separate policy choice — they're waiting because 610.40(g) makes "wait" the rule and
"release early" the narrow, documented exception.

And the rule that actually fires on Wednesday's reactive result, quoted verbatim from the same
source:

> (h) *Restrictions on shipment or use* — (1) *Reactive screening test.* You must not ship or use
> human blood or blood components that have a reactive screening test for evidence of infection
> due to relevant transfusion-transmitted infection(s) designated in paragraph (a) of this
> section or that are collected from a donor with a previous record of a reactive screening test
> for evidence of infection due to relevant transfusion-transmitted infection(s) designated in
> paragraph (a) of this section, except as provided in paragraphs (h)(2)(i) through (h)(2)(vii)
> of this section.

That prohibition attaches to "blood or blood components" — plural, and not scoped to whichever
product happens to still be sitting in the testing lab's fridge. It reaches the platelets in the
agitator and the plasma in the freezer exactly as much as it reaches a hypothetical unit that
hadn't been processed yet. The text later cross-references § 610.41 as the regulation governing
the donor's own deferral once a reactive result is confirmed — the donor side of Wednesday's
consequence, running alongside the product side.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator reconstructing Wednesday's reactive result doesn't ask Lakeshore to describe
its quarantine philosophy. They ask for three things, and a gap in any one is a finding on its
own.

**The donation record showing the single donor number**, and every product record that traces
back to it — proof that Lakeshore's system actually resolved "platelets in the agitator," "plasma
in the freezer," and "red cells in the refrigerator" as the same donation, per 606.160(c), rather
than three separate lookups someone had to do manually.

**A timestamped quarantine action on all three products**, not just the one that happened to
still be in the testing lab. If the platelets' quarantine flag was set at a different time than
the plasma's, or later than the moment the result posted, that gap — however small — is exactly
the finding an investigator is trained to look for, because it's the gap where a unit could have
shipped.

**The donor notification and, if applicable, the lookback record.** 606.160(b)(1)(viii) — from
the same source already in this course's `sources/cfr/606.160.md` — requires records of
"quarantine; consignee notification; testing; notification of a transfusion recipient... and
disposition" performed under the regulations governing reactive-donor followup. An investigator
expects to see this chain complete: not just "the platelets were destroyed," but who was told,
when, and what happened to every prior donation from that donor that might also need review.

A bad answer to "how do you know all three products got quarantined, not just the one in the
lab" sounds like "the technician who saw the result would have called processing." That describes
a hope, not a control. The control an inspector is looking for is a system-wide status check keyed
to the donation number, not a phone call that depends on someone remembering where the other two
products went.

## Common traps

**"If the components are already separated and sitting in storage, testing must already be
done."** This is exactly backwards, and it's the trap this module's scenario is built to catch.
Component separation and infectious-disease testing run in parallel, not in sequence — Lakeshore
routinely has fully processed, physically ready products sitting in storage while their sample
tubes are still in the testing lab. The parallelism isn't a shortcut or a compliance gap; it's
normal operational necessity, made safe entirely by the quarantine status attached to the
donation number, not by any assumption about how far along processing has gotten.

**"A negative result on one test in the panel clears the whole thing."** The infectious-disease
panel under 610.40(a) covers several distinct infections, each with its own test — a negative HIV
result says nothing about the hepatitis C result, which may still be pending or may come back
reactive on its own. Release requires every required test in the panel to be complete and
passing, per 610.40(g)'s framing of testing completion as the condition for release — not "the
tests we've gotten back so far look fine."

## What this means for your job

- **Ask how quarantine status propagates the moment a result posts, not just how it's recorded.**
  A system that correctly flags the unit in the testing lab's own inventory but takes an overnight
  batch job to flag the same donation's components sitting elsewhere has a real window where a
  product could ship. Ask for the actual latency, not the intended design.
- **Don't accept "someone would have caught it" for multi-product donations.** The moment a
  donation is split into components, the question stops being "is the unit on hold" and becomes
  "are all of its products on hold, everywhere they physically are." That's a systems question, not
  a staffing question.
- **Know that a reactive result is at minimum three separate obligations, not one.** Product
  disposition, donor deferral, and donor notification (and possibly lookback into that donor's
  prior donations) all fire off the same trigger. If your Quality Analyst's report only closes out
  the product side, ask what happened on the donor side.
- **Treat the donation identifier as the single source of truth for "what does this result
  apply to."** If two systems — say, the processing lab's inventory and the testing lab's LIS
  (laboratory information system) — can disagree about which products trace back to a given
  donation number, that's a data-integrity gap with the same shape as the unmerged donor record
  from module 1, just on the product side instead of the identity side.
- **When a vendor or process change touches how quarantine status is set or checked, ask what
  happens to products that were already released to a different workflow stage before the change.**
  A gate that only checks status at one point in the pipeline isn't a gate; it's a gate at one
  intersection on a road with several on-ramps.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Wednesday's test comes back reactive. What actually has to happen, and to what?

At minimum: every product derived from Tuesday's donation — the red cells, the plasma, and the
platelets, wherever each physically is — must be quarantined or destroyed under 610.40(h)(1),
found via the single donor number required by 606.160(c). Separately, the donor is deferred (the
regulation governing that deferral, § 610.41, is cross-referenced directly inside 610.40(h)) and
must be notified, the same notification obligation module 1 covered for eligibility deferrals,
now triggered by a reactive test instead. Depending on which test was reactive, Lakeshore may also
have to review the donor's prior donations for lookback. It's a product-side action and at least
two donor-side actions, not just "throw away the unit."
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Lakeshore's platelets were fully processed and sitting in storage a full day before the testing panel finished. Is that sequence itself a compliance problem?

No — and this is worth being precise about, because it's not what 610.40 actually regulates.
Nothing in 610.40 requires processing to wait for testing to finish; it requires that *release or
shipment* wait for testing to finish (610.40(g)), with narrow, documented exceptions. Processing
components ahead of a testing result is normal blood-center operations, not a shortcut around the
rule. The compliance question is never "did processing start before testing finished" — it's
"did anything move past quarantine before the gate opened." Confusing the two is exactly the trap
this module opens with.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A sample tube gets mislabeled during Tuesday's draw, but the collection bag itself is labeled correctly. Is that a minor paperwork issue, since the physical product isn't affected?

No. 606.160(c) is what makes a test result on a sample tube mean anything at all for the products
made from that donation — it's the record that relates the tube, the bag, the donor, and every
component back to one number. A mislabeled tube breaks that link at its weakest point: either the
wrong result gets associated with this donation's products, or this donation's own result never
gets matched to them, and either failure defeats the entire testing-and-quarantine system
regardless of how correct the bag's own label is. The identity link is what gives a test result
its meaning; a tube-level identity error is a testing-system failure, not a clerical one.
:::

## Where this goes next

Tuesday's donation, if it clears every result, is now three correctly identified, correctly
quarantined-then-released products — but they're still bulk components without their final
labels, without modifications like leukoreduction or irradiation applied, and without the
expiration dating that depends on exactly which component they are. Module 3,
`component-processing-and-labeling`, picks up from here: how one donation becomes several
distinct products with different shelf lives, what has to happen to a component before it's
eligible for release into inventory, and the full ISBT 128 standard behind the barcode that the
DIN mentioned in this module is only the first piece of.
